The lab smelled of cold coffee and toner. It was 11:40 p.m., and the grant submission was due at 5 a.m., and the figure was on the monitor in a state Dr. Okafor had only seen in her own dreams: clean. Too clean. The error bars sat like small, obedient hands folded in their laps, and the regression line threaded through the data the way a river threads through a valley it had already chosen.

She had not built that river. She had carved it.

Two points. Just two. The ones from the Yonsei replicates that had arrived three weeks late with a note in Korean she hadn't yet had the energy to translate. Two points that, if left in, would have buckled the slope into something the review panel would have called "suggestive" rather than "confirmed." Two points that, in the architecture of her mind at 2 a.m. the previous night, had looked less like data and more like a hand reaching through the glass to close the door on her.

She had dragged them into the Recycle Bin. She had not looked at the Recycle Bin again.

The door clicked. Dr. Mensah walked in without his coat, holding a paper cup, and stood behind her chair with the particular stillness of a man who already knows what he is about to say.

"Is this all of the data we collected?" he asked.

The question was not an accusation. It was worse. It was a question the way a key is a key: quiet, mechanical, turning in a lock she had not known was still locked. The cursor blinked on the figure. The regression line waited.

Dr. Okafor did not turn in her chair. She kept her eyes on the screen, on the two empty spaces where the points had been, two small absences the size of her own pulse.

"I deleted the Yonsei replicates from the figure," she said. Her voice was flat, the voice she used when a student's pipette slipped and she needed to explain to the floor that nothing had broken, that the solution was still stable, that the experiment could proceed. "I deleted them because the slope would have changed, and if the slope changed, the panel would have asked for a second year, and I don't have a second year. I have a lease. I have three postdocs whose funding is tied to this. I have a mother in Enugu who thinks I am doing the work and not the work, and I don't have the words to tell her the difference." She turned then, just enough for him to see her face. "I will put them back. I will put them back tonight, and I will build the figure again, and I will submit it at 4:55 and let the panel see what the river actually looks like when it's allowed to choose its own valley. But I need you to understand that I did it because I was afraid, not because I believed they didn't belong."

Dr. Mensah set his paper cup on the desk. He did not say *I understand.* He opened a new file and began, in silence, to pull the two points back in.

The coffee had gone a full hour cold. Neither of them made a new cup.

Dr. Adaeze Okafor sat at her desk with the grant narrative open in one window and Figure 4 in the other, the scatter plot rendered in the particular shade of blue she'd chosen because the reviewers' demographic favored it. She'd been staring at the figure for an hour. The two points were gone. Not deleted—she'd checked; they were still in the raw CSV, sitting in a folder she'd named *hold* with the kind of deliberateness that made the word feel like a verdict.

Her phone buzzed. Not a text. A call.

"Adaeze." Marcus Chen's voice had the flatness of a man who had just opened a PDF at his kitchen table and found something wrong. "I was doing the supplemental materials. I pulled the raw collection log. There are forty-seven data points logged for the dose-response run. Your Figure 4 has forty-five."

The hum of the lab's ventilation system filled the silence. Outside, the streetlight on Ninth Street had begun its seasonal flicker, throwing intermittent amber across the window.

Adaeze set the figure aside. She pulled her cardigan tighter, though the room was warm.

"Marcus. It's eleven-forty."

"The deadline is tomorrow at five." A pause. "Is this all of the data we collected?"

She closed her eyes. Behind her eyelids she saw the two points sitting in the lower-right corner of the plot, stubborn as knots in wood, dragging the regression line three degrees off the trend. She saw the funding threshold in the panel rubric. She saw Yemi's face at the faculty meeting in March, where the department chair had said the lab would need to demonstrate "sustained statistical viability" or the instrument allocation would be redistributed.

"Those two points," she said. Then, because the first sentence had not been the one she needed, she started over, quieter, as if speaking to herself through the phone: "They came from the batch where we switched the substrate lot. I ran the batch control and it read 112 percent. I didn't want the panel to spend their review looking at a batch error. I didn't want them to say the curve is a suggestion." She stopped. Swallowed. "If I leave them in, the R-squared goes to 0.61. And I looked at the criteria, Marcus. I looked, and I thought, if they don't fund this cycle, Yemi's cohort doesn't finish in the spring. And I didn't—I couldn't sleep. So I put them in a folder and told myself I would look at them again in the morning."

The line was quiet for a long time.

"You can move them back in the raw file," Marcus said finally. "I'll flag the batch annotation in the methods. We annotate. We explain. We don't—" He stopped himself. "Come to the lab. I'll make coffee."

Adaeze looked at the figure. The blue points held their position as if they had always been there, patient and complete.

"Twenty minutes," she said.

The figure had been perfect for eleven hours. Dr. Chidi Okafor remembered the exact moment the perfection became a problem: 2:14 a.m., a Thursday, the second data point from the left edge of the graph winking at her from the scatter plot like an accusation. She'd highlighted it, hit delete, and then, because the first deletion made the second one look *convenient*, she'd taken that one too. The curve smoothed. The story held. The R01, due to the institute by 11:59 p.m. the following night, would tell a story about a mechanism she was almost certain existed.

She did not sleep.

At 7:42, her co-author, Lena, set a mug of terrible breakroom coffee on the corner of Okafor's desk without a word and sat in the guest chair with the posture of someone who had already made a decision and was waiting for confirmation.

Lena had been looking at the figure for four minutes. Okafor knew because she'd been watching Lena watch the figure, reading the slow shift in her jaw.

"Is this all of the data we collected?"

The question was not a question. It was a door being opened in a room Okafor had been standing in the dark.

Okafor set down the pen she'd been holding. She looked at the ceiling, where a fluorescent tube had been flickering since March, and when she spoke, her voice came out lower than she intended, as though she were explaining something to a student who had asked too early.

"No. And I'm not going to tell you I made a mistake. I made a choice. I looked at those two points, and I thought: if I leave them in, the story we're telling doesn't hold, and the R01 doesn't get funded, and this lab doesn't get the next three years, and four postdocs walk out into a spring they weren't promised. I know. I know what you're going to say. I *know.* But I put them back. They're in the supplemental file, tagged. I'm going to tell the reviewers, in the cover letter, that we observed two anomalies we couldn't account for in the current model, and that we're investigating them before scaling the mechanism to the full cohort. I'm not hiding them. I'm *sequencing* them. Is that a distinction you can live with? I don't know if it's enough. I need you to tell me it's enough before I can sleep tonight, because I will not sleep tonight if you look at me the way you're looking at me right now."

Lena picked up the coffee. Took a sip. Set it back down, untouched.

"Come to my office at nine," she said. "We'll write the cover letter together."

It was not an absolution. But Okafor closed her laptop, and for the first time in eleven hours, her hands were still.

The ribbon on the finish line was the color of a bruise — that mottled purple the organizers had chosen because it matched the year's charity gala theme, and nobody had thought to ask if it looked like a wound. Lena stepped over it anyway, arms raised, the crowd beyond the inflatable arches doing the thing where they clap a little too loud, a little too long, as if the half-marathon were a coronation.

Her official time: 1:38:42. Fast enough for the office prize. Fast enough that Derek from Accounting, who had pre-registered last week in a windbreaker two sizes too large, later told his team she'd "basically stolen the thing."

She hadn't stolen it. She'd just... shortened it.

The east loop. That stupid, beautiful stretch where the course doubled back through the wetlands and added four miles to a route the map still showed as a clean little rectangle. Lena had known about the gap — the missing mile markers, the way the volunteer in the yellow vest stood at the wrong tree. At mile nine, with her calves going to concrete and the November wind pulling at her ponytail like a child testing a gate, she'd turned left. Just left. Just once.

She'd made herself feel like a cheat at a board game. She'd made herself feel like a kid who skipped the last page of a novel.

Now, three weeks later, the office had become a kind of tribunal. Derek stood behind the water cooler in the break room, holding a small glass plaque — the office prize, engraved with Lena's name and the time. He set it on the laminate counter between them with the careful hands of a man placing a live grenade.

"Congratulations, Lena."

"Thanks, Derek."

He didn't leave. He folded his arms over the windbreaker he'd apparently never taken off. The break room hummed its low fluorescent hum. Somewhere down the hall, a printer burped.

"You ran the full course, right?"

The question landed flat. No preamble, no gentle circling. Just the words, laid on the counter next to the plaque like a second object to be weighed.

Lena looked at the glass. Her name caught the light. She turned it over, looked at the engraving on the reverse — a small line of text in the company's serif font. She turned it back.

"No," she said. "I didn't. I took the shortcut on the east loop. I'm not making excuses, and I'm not going to tell you it was a mistake I didn't notice. I saw the gap and I chose it." She set the plaque down. "I'm sorry. The money goes where it's supposed to go, and I'll run the full course next year, legs or no legs. But I won't pretend I earned this." She tapped the glass. "I just... needed those four minutes. And I'm not proud of how I got them."

Derek was quiet for a long time. Then he picked up the plaque, turned it over in his hands, and set it back down.

"Okay," he said. "I just needed to know."

He walked back toward the printer. The windbreaker swished.

Lena stayed in the break room for another eleven minutes, sitting on the edge of a conference table, the glass plaque cold under her fingers, waiting for her stomach to decide whether it wanted to be grateful or ashamed.

It chose both.

The trend line arced exactly where the grant narrative needed it to arc.

She had deleted the two points at 11:47 p.m., during a stretch where she could no longer see her own face in the monitor and kept blinking at the spreadsheet like it owed her an apology. The two points were replicates from the secondary chamber. They sat below the threshold, pulling the slope flat in a way that made the entire Phase II projection look, in Dr. Okafor's exhausted words, "a little less miraculous."

She told herself she would re-run them in the morning. She told herself this at 11:52, 12:03, and 1:15, each time with a little less conviction than the last.

A key turned in the door at 1:48 a.m. Nora leaned against the frame in a rain-damp coat, coffee in both hands, and set one cup on the counter. She did not sit. She pulled a stool up to the desk where the figure was still open, zoomed, the two missing coordinates marked in faint red in the raw data log.

"Is this all of the data we collected?"

The question landed without inflection. Not an accusation. Not a sigh. Just a question, the way you'd ask if the car was parked or if the stove was off.

Dr. Okafor set down the granola bar. She wiped her hands on the back of her lab coat, a gesture so automatic it might have been a reflex, a muscle memory from years of pretending her work was tidy when it was not.

"Those two points," she said, and her voice came out thin, scraped, like a wire pulled over a surface too many times. "They were from the secondary chamber. The one with the gasket seal that's been off since Tuesday. I thought they were instrument drift. I thought—" She stopped. Swallowed. "I didn't verify that. Not properly. I just pulled them and I told myself I'd run the chamber back in the morning and if they reproduced, I'd put them in, and if they didn't, they'd be a known artifact." A pause long enough for the fluorescent light to buzz twice. "And I haven't run them back. The deadline is in nine hours and I'm three hours into a night where I can't make myself open the raw file again. So they're not in the figure. And I don't have an explanation for that besides what I just gave you. Which isn't one."

Nora picked up the coffee. Took a long sip. Did not set it down.

"Nine hours," Nora repeated, softly. "Okay. We fix the figure. We re-run the chamber at four. And if the points come back the same way—"

"They come back the same way," Dr. Okafor said. It was not a question. It was the sound of a door closing on a room she had been hiding in for four hours. "They come back the same way."

Nora nodded once. Poured the second cup. Set it in front of Dr. Okafor, still hot, still whole, as if the night could be poured back into the morning.

"Then we rewrite the projection. Tonight."

Dr. Okafor wrapped both hands around the cup. The heat seeped through the paper and into her palms and she did not open the file. Not yet. She let the number sit on the counter between them, unexamined, for as long as she could.

Then she did.
